Overview

Warsaw as a Business Centre

Warsaw is Poland's capital and its principal business centre. Statistics Poland recorded 1,863,845 residents at the end of 2024, and the city's economy was estimated at around one-sixth of national GDP in 2019. It is home to the Warsaw Stock Exchange (GPW), the largest equity trading platform in central and eastern Europe, to both houses of parliament and the central government, and to the head offices of most major Polish banks and many international groups. Services dominate employment, and the city hosts more than 300 business services centres, most created by foreign investors, covering shared services, IT, outsourcing and research and development.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Warsaw because it is where Polish deals, regulators and disputes concentrate. Investors and lenders want to understand who stands behind a Polish target or counterparty and whether its history matches its presentation. Multinationals running finance, IT or procurement functions from Warsaw service centres face the misconduct risks that come with large, distributed back offices: vendor fraud, conflicts of interest and data leaving with departing staff. As the seat of central government, Warsaw is also where public procurement and regulatory exposure arise, and where many commercial cases and arbitrations are heard, so counsel need well-sourced facts.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Warsaw

01

Polish counterparty and investor diligence

Researching Warsaw-based companies, investors and their principals before acquisitions, joint ventures or financing, using National Court Register filings, financial statements, press, litigation information and Polish-language open sources to test ownership, management history, related-party links and reputation.

02

Business services centre misconduct

Supporting counsel investigating suspected vendor fraud, invoice manipulation, conflicts of interest or data theft at a Warsaw shared services or IT centre, with background research on suppliers and connected individuals and an inquiry structured to respect GDPR and Polish employment law.

03

Public procurement and integrity risk

Assessing integrity risk around bidders, subcontractors and intermediaries in public contracts awarded by central institutions and state-owned companies headquartered in Warsaw, including ownership links, prior disputes and adverse media, to inform compliance decisions and anti-corruption programmes.

04

Listed company and shareholder research

Background research on companies listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange and on significant shareholders, including disclosed holdings, management changes, related entities and reported disputes, for investors, activists or counsel evaluating governance concerns or contested transactions.

05

Arbitration and litigation fact support

Assembling factual records for counsel in commercial disputes seated in Warsaw, whether before the commercial divisions of the Warsaw courts or an arbitral tribunal, including counterparties' corporate histories, assets disclosed in public sources and witness identification.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Warsaw

Warsaw courts

Warsaw has the full hierarchy of Polish courts: district courts, the Regional Court in Warsaw with dedicated commercial divisions, and the Court of Appeal in Warsaw, alongside the Supreme Court and the Supreme Administrative Court, which both sit in the city. Because many Polish groups and state-owned companies are registered in Warsaw, a large share of significant commercial litigation is heard there. Searching court calendars and judgments involving a counterparty is a standard part of dispute-history research.

Court of Arbitration at KIG

The Court of Arbitration at the Polish Chamber of Commerce (SA KIG) in Warsaw traces its history to 1 January 1950, when it was founded to settle foreign trade disputes, and has been part of the Chamber since 1990. It handles roughly 300 to 600 cases a year, nearly 20 percent with an international dimension, under rules in force since 2015. The Lewiatan Court of Arbitration also operates in Warsaw. Investigative support is limited to factual research for counsel and the parties.

Financial market institutions

The Warsaw Stock Exchange, which marked thirty years in 2021, publishes listed-company reports and disclosures that are a core source on Polish issuers. The Polish Financial Supervision Authority (KNF), which supervises banking, capital markets, insurance and pensions, is also based in Warsaw, and its published decisions and warnings can be relevant when assessing financial-sector counterparties.

Registers and the Warsaw business base

Companies headquartered in Warsaw are entered in the National Court Register through the registry divisions of the Warsaw district courts, with extracts and filed financial statements available online nationwide. Land and mortgage registers (księgi wieczyste) can be consulted online by register number. Because so many holding companies and foreign-owned subsidiaries use Warsaw addresses, confirming whether a registered office reflects real operations is often necessary.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Warsaw

For matters touching Warsaw, TDSC starts by fixing the decision the client faces, such as whether to invest, whom to contract with or how to respond to suspected misconduct, and then identifies which Warsaw registers, courts, exchange disclosures and regulators are relevant. Research is conducted from Nashville in Polish and English using lawful public and commercial sources. Where document retrieval, site visits or interviews are justified, TDSC coordinates with appropriately licensed Polish detectives under the Act on detective services and with the client's Polish counsel, rather than acting directly. Personal data is processed under GDPR principles, limited to the purpose, and inquiries at Warsaw service centres are designed with counsel to respect employee rights.

TDSC has no office in Warsaw. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope.

Questions

Warsaw: Frequently Asked Questions

Can you look into a supplier to our Warsaw shared services centre?

Yes. We research the supplier's registration, ownership, management, financial filings and litigation history, and look for links to your own staff or former staff where the facts suggest a conflict of interest. Any review of employee data is planned with your counsel so that it has a lawful basis under GDPR and Polish labour law.

What can Warsaw Stock Exchange disclosures tell us about a Polish company?

Listed issuers publish periodic and current reports covering results, significant contracts, shareholder changes and disputes. These help reconstruct a company's history and connections. We compare them with register filings, press and court information, and note where disclosures stop short, for example on private affiliates or shareholders below reporting thresholds.

Do you support arbitrations before the Court of Arbitration at the Polish Chamber of Commerce?

We support counsel, not the tribunal. Typical tasks include researching the opposing party's corporate group, its prior disputes and assets visible in public sources, and identifying former employees or other potential witnesses. We do not give legal advice on procedure or the merits; that remains with Polish counsel.

Is public procurement in Warsaw a particular focus?

Central government ministries and many state-owned companies are headquartered in Warsaw, so contracts they award are a frequent subject of integrity screening. We research bidders, subcontractors and intermediaries for hidden ownership, political exposure and adverse history, giving compliance teams a factual basis for their decisions.

Does TDSC have an office in Warsaw?

No. TDSC is based in Nashville and has no office or staff in Poland. Most work is desk research. Where on-the-ground steps are needed, we coordinate with licensed Polish detectives and the client's counsel, and we decline requests that would involve restricted records, covert recording or methods reserved to state authorities.
